content_sba.stem: Minutes after receiving cefazolin, a 28-year-old develops diffuse urticaria, wheezing, facial swelling, and hypotension. Help has been called and the patient is positioned safely.
content_sba.lead_in: Which medication and route should be given first?

rationales.correct_answer: Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line because it rapidly treats airway edema, bronchospasm, and circulatory collapse.

B.why_wrong: An antihistamine does not reverse shock or upper-airway obstruction and must not delay epinephrine.

C.why_tempting: Albuterol can improve bronchospasm and wheeze.
C.why_wrong: It is an adjunct that does not treat airway edema or hypotension.

D.why_wrong: Its onset is delayed and it is not acute rescue therapy.

explanation.level_1: Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line because it rapidly treats airway edema, bronchospasm, and circulatory collapse.

level_2.A: Intramuscular epinephrine is first-line because it rapidly treats airway edema, bronchospasm, and circulatory collapse.
level_2.B: Diphenhydramine can improve urticaria. An antihistamine does not reverse shock or upper-airway obstruction and must not delay epinephrine.
level_2.C: Albuterol can improve bronchospasm and wheeze. It is an adjunct that does not treat airway edema or hypotension.
level_2.D: A corticosteroid targets inflammation. Its onset is delayed and it is not acute rescue therapy.

clinical_pearls: Do not delay epinephrine while administering antihistamines or corticosteroids.
Initial epinephrine is given intramuscularly; routine IV bolus administration carries greater cardiovascular risk.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests recognition of the only first-line medication for a multisystem anaphylactic emergency.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Demonstrates decisive prioritization of an immediately life-saving intervention.
common_traps: Treating the rash or wheeze first
Delaying epinephrine while seeking confirmatory testing

content_sba.stem: A 72-year-old with atrial fibrillation at 180/min has crushing chest pain, pulmonary edema, and a blood pressure of 76/44 mm Hg. The instability is attributable to the tachyarrhythmia, and a pulse is present.
content_sba.lead_in: Which immediate treatment is indicated?

rationales.correct_answer: Atrial fibrillation that is causing hemodynamic instability requires prompt synchronized electrical cardioversion.

A.why_tempting: Diltiazem is used for ventricular rate control in selected stable patients.
A.why_wrong: It may worsen hypotension and delays the indicated electrical treatment.

C.why_tempting: Digoxin can slow atrioventricular nodal conduction.
C.why_wrong: Its onset is too slow for shock and pulmonary edema caused by the rhythm.

D.why_tempting: Defibrillation is a familiar emergency electrical treatment.
D.why_wrong: Unsynchronized shock is for pulseless or unsynchronizable malignant rhythms, not atrial fibrillation with a pulse.

explanation.level_1: Atrial fibrillation that is causing hemodynamic instability requires prompt synchronized electrical cardioversion.

level_2.A: Diltiazem is used for ventricular rate control in selected stable patients. It may worsen hypotension and delays the indicated electrical treatment.
level_2.B: Atrial fibrillation that is causing hemodynamic instability requires prompt synchronized electrical cardioversion.
level_2.C: Digoxin can slow atrioventricular nodal conduction. Its onset is too slow for shock and pulmonary edema caused by the rhythm.
level_2.D: Defibrillation is a familiar emergency electrical treatment. Unsynchronized shock is for pulseless or unsynchronizable malignant rhythms, not atrial fibrillation with a pulse.

clinical_pearls: First decide whether the tachyarrhythmia is causing the instability rather than accompanying another cause.
A pulse plus rhythm-caused instability is the cue for synchronization.
level_3.board_relevance: Distinguishes the unstable tachyarrhythmia pathway from routine rate control.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Tests whether the candidate can name and justify an urgent intervention without being distracted by standard stable-patient therapy.
common_traps: Choosing rate control despite shock
Confusing synchronized cardioversion with defibrillation

content_sba.stem: Several family members develop headache and confusion after indoor generator use. One patient’s conventional pulse oximeter reads 99% after supplemental oxygen is started.
content_sba.lead_in: Which test best supports the suspected diagnosis?

rationales.correct_answer: Carboxyhemoglobin measured with multiwavelength co-oximetry supports carbon monoxide poisoning; arterial or venous blood may be used.

A.why_tempting: Arterial oxygen tension directly measures dissolved oxygen.
A.why_wrong: It can be normal despite impaired hemoglobin oxygen carriage and does not measure carboxyhemoglobin.

B.why_tempting: Methemoglobinemia is another cause of abnormal hemoglobin oxygen handling.
B.why_wrong: It is a different dyshemoglobinemia and does not confirm carbon monoxide exposure.

D.why_tempting: Lactate may rise with systemic toxicity.
D.why_wrong: It is neither specific for nor confirmatory of carbon monoxide poisoning.

explanation.level_1: Carboxyhemoglobin measured with multiwavelength co-oximetry supports carbon monoxide poisoning; arterial or venous blood may be used.

level_2.A: Arterial oxygen tension directly measures dissolved oxygen. It can be normal despite impaired hemoglobin oxygen carriage and does not measure carboxyhemoglobin.
level_2.B: Methemoglobinemia is another cause of abnormal hemoglobin oxygen handling. It is a different dyshemoglobinemia and does not confirm carbon monoxide exposure.
level_2.C: Carboxyhemoglobin measured with multiwavelength co-oximetry supports carbon monoxide poisoning; arterial or venous blood may be used.
level_2.D: Lactate may rise with systemic toxicity. It is neither specific for nor confirmatory of carbon monoxide poisoning.

clinical_pearls: A conventional two-wavelength pulse oximeter can be falsely reassuring.
Interpret carboxyhemoglobin in light of elapsed time and oxygen already administered; severity remains a clinical assessment.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests the classic limitation of conventional pulse oximetry in dyshemoglobinemia.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Rewards candidates who explain why an apparently normal monitor does not override exposure history and symptoms.

Using carboxyhemoglobin alone to grade clinical severity

content_sba.stem: An adult has continued generalized tonic-clonic activity for 7 minutes. Glucose is normal, airway support is underway, and intravenous access is available.
content_sba.lead_in: Which medication is the preferred initial antiseizure treatment?

rationales.correct_answer: A benzodiazepine such as intravenous lorazepam is preferred initial therapy during the 5-to-20-minute treatment phase.

A.why_tempting: Fosphenytoin is an accepted second-phase antiseizure agent.
A.why_wrong: It should not replace an adequate initial benzodiazepine.

B.why_tempting: Levetiracetam is commonly used after benzodiazepine therapy.
B.why_wrong: It is a second-phase option, not the preferred initial drug here.

C.why_tempting: Valproate is another evidence-supported second-phase option.
C.why_wrong: It also follows rather than precedes initial benzodiazepine therapy.

explanation.level_1: A benzodiazepine such as intravenous lorazepam is preferred initial therapy during the 5-to-20-minute treatment phase.

level_2.A: Fosphenytoin is an accepted second-phase antiseizure agent. It should not replace an adequate initial benzodiazepine.
level_2.B: Levetiracetam is commonly used after benzodiazepine therapy. It is a second-phase option, not the preferred initial drug here.
level_2.C: Valproate is another evidence-supported second-phase option. It also follows rather than precedes initial benzodiazepine therapy.
level_2.D: A benzodiazepine such as intravenous lorazepam is preferred initial therapy during the 5-to-20-minute treatment phase.

clinical_pearls: Treat ongoing convulsive activity once it reaches 5 minutes.
Fosphenytoin, levetiracetam, and valproate are second-phase options after adequate benzodiazepine treatment.

content_sba.stem: A pregnant patient has confirmed primary syphilis and reports an immediate-type penicillin allergy.
content_sba.lead_in: Which management best treats maternal infection and prevents congenital syphilis?

choices.text: Use azithromycin and repeat serology in four weeks
Desensitize, then give stage-appropriate penicillin G
Use doxycycline now and defer penicillin until after delivery
Use ceftriaxone and omit penicillin throughout pregnancy

rationales.correct_answer: Penicillin is the only therapy with documented efficacy for preventing fetal infection; an allergic pregnant patient should be desensitized and then treated with stage-appropriate penicillin G.

A.why_tempting: Azithromycin is orally administered and active against some bacterial infections.
A.why_wrong: It does not reliably cure maternal syphilis or treat the fetus.

C.why_tempting: Doxycycline can be used for syphilis in selected nonpregnant patients.
C.why_wrong: It is not the recommended solution during pregnancy.

D.why_tempting: Ceftriaxone has activity against Treponema pallidum.
D.why_wrong: Evidence is insufficient to rely on it for prevention of congenital syphilis.

explanation.level_1: Penicillin is the only therapy with documented efficacy for preventing fetal infection; an allergic pregnant patient should be desensitized and then treated with stage-appropriate penicillin G.

level_2.A: Azithromycin is orally administered and active against some bacterial infections. It does not reliably cure maternal syphilis or treat the fetus.
level_2.B: Penicillin is the only therapy with documented efficacy for preventing fetal infection; an allergic pregnant patient should be desensitized and then treated with stage-appropriate penicillin G.
level_2.C: Doxycycline can be used for syphilis in selected nonpregnant patients. It is not the recommended solution during pregnancy.
level_2.D: Ceftriaxone has activity against Treponema pallidum. Evidence is insufficient to rely on it for prevention of congenital syphilis.

clinical_pearls: Pregnancy removes the usual alternative-antibiotic pathway for penicillin allergy.
Fetal ultrasound can inform management later in pregnancy but must not delay maternal treatment.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests a high-yield exception in which desensitization is required because no equivalent alternative exists.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Demonstrates maternal-fetal risk prioritization and recognition of when allergy workarounds are unsafe.
common_traps: Choosing a standard nonpregnant alternative
Delaying treatment for fetal imaging
level_3.memory_aid: Pregnant plus syphilis: make penicillin possible.

content_sba.stem: An adult has fever, neck stiffness, altered mental status, papilledema, and a focal neurologic deficit. Cranial imaging is required before lumbar puncture.
content_sba.lead_in: Which next action is most appropriate?

choices.text: Defer antimicrobials until after imaging and lumbar puncture
Draw blood cultures and start empiric IV antibiotics now

rationales.correct_answer: When lumbar puncture is deferred for imaging, obtain blood cultures promptly and start empiric antibacterial therapy without waiting for imaging or cerebrospinal-fluid results.

A.why_tempting: Pretreatment cerebrospinal fluid can improve diagnostic yield.
A.why_wrong: A dangerous treatment delay outweighs that benefit when bacterial meningitis is suspected.

B.why_tempting: Altered mental status and focal findings can raise concern for encephalitis.
B.why_wrong: Acyclovir alone does not treat suspected bacterial meningitis.

D.why_tempting: Dexamethasone may be given with or just before initial antibacterial therapy in appropriate suspected bacterial meningitis.
D.why_wrong: It is an adjunct and cannot replace immediate empiric antibacterial treatment.

explanation.level_1: When lumbar puncture is deferred for imaging, obtain blood cultures promptly and start empiric antibacterial therapy without waiting for imaging or cerebrospinal-fluid results.

level_2.A: Pretreatment cerebrospinal fluid can improve diagnostic yield. A dangerous treatment delay outweighs that benefit when bacterial meningitis is suspected.
level_2.B: Altered mental status and focal findings can raise concern for encephalitis. Acyclovir alone does not treat suspected bacterial meningitis.
level_2.C: When lumbar puncture is deferred for imaging, obtain blood cultures promptly and start empiric antibacterial therapy without waiting for imaging or cerebrospinal-fluid results.
level_2.D: Dexamethasone may be given with or just before initial antibacterial therapy in appropriate suspected bacterial meningitis. It is an adjunct and cannot replace immediate empiric antibacterial treatment.

clinical_pearls: Draw blood cultures first only when doing so causes no meaningful delay.
The exact empiric regimen depends on age, immune status, epidemiology, and local resistance.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests the non-delay principle when neuroimaging must precede lumbar puncture.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Assesses whether the candidate can parallel-process diagnostics and treatment in a time-critical infection.
common_traps: Waiting for imaging before antimicrobials

content_sba.stem: A hemodynamically stable patient with cirrhosis is admitted with a first episode of clinically apparent ascites.
content_sba.lead_in: Which next step is most appropriate?

choices.text: Use contrast CT as the sole diagnostic test
Start empiric antibiotics without fluid sampling
Perform diagnostic paracentesis with fluid studies

rationales.correct_answer: New-onset clinically apparent ascites should be sampled with diagnostic paracentesis to assess cause and identify infection when present.

A.why_tempting: Diuretics are commonly used for cirrhotic ascites.
A.why_wrong: Treatment does not replace initial etiologic and infection assessment.

B.why_tempting: CT can identify structural abdominal disease.
B.why_wrong: Imaging may supplement but does not replace diagnostic fluid analysis.

C.why_wrong: A stable patient should be sampled promptly so treatment can be guided by clinical and fluid findings.

explanation.level_1: New-onset clinically apparent ascites should be sampled with diagnostic paracentesis to assess cause and identify infection when present.

level_2.A: Diuretics are commonly used for cirrhotic ascites. Treatment does not replace initial etiologic and infection assessment.
level_2.B: CT can identify structural abdominal disease. Imaging may supplement but does not replace diagnostic fluid analysis.
level_2.C: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis is dangerous. A stable patient should be sampled promptly so treatment can be guided by clinical and fluid findings.
level_2.D: New-onset clinically apparent ascites should be sampled with diagnostic paracentesis to assess cause and identify infection when present.

clinical_pearls: Hospital admission strengthens the need to exclude spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.
Initial studies commonly include cell count, albumin, total protein, and culture when indicated.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests the first diagnostic procedure for accessible new fluid in cirrhosis.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Shows disciplined diagnostic sequencing before reflexively escalating chronic therapy.

content_sba.stem: A patient has severe thrombocytopenia, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes, neurologic symptoms, and otherwise unexplained near-normal coagulation studies. A pretreatment ADAMTS13 sample has been sent, clinical suspicion for immune TTP is high, and therapeutic plasma exchange is immediately available.
content_sba.lead_in: Which initial treatment is indicated?

choices.text: Rituximab plus corticosteroids without plasma exchange

rationales.correct_answer: Suspected acute immune TTP is life-threatening, so therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids should begin urgently after the diagnostic sample is obtained rather than await ADAMTS13 results.

B.why_tempting: Severe thrombocytopenia can prompt consideration of platelet transfusion.
B.why_wrong: Platelets do not treat the underlying thrombotic microangiopathy and are generally avoided without compelling life-threatening bleeding.

C.why_wrong: Plasma infusion alone is not adequate definitive treatment for acute immune TTP when plasma exchange is available.

D.why_tempting: Rituximab can be an adjunct in immune TTP.
D.why_wrong: It does not replace emergency plasma exchange and corticosteroids.

explanation.level_1: Suspected acute immune TTP is life-threatening, so therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids should begin urgently after the diagnostic sample is obtained rather than await ADAMTS13 results.

level_2.A: Suspected acute immune TTP is life-threatening, so therapeutic plasma exchange and corticosteroids should begin urgently after the diagnostic sample is obtained rather than await ADAMTS13 results.
level_2.B: Severe thrombocytopenia can prompt consideration of platelet transfusion. Platelets do not treat the underlying thrombotic microangiopathy and are generally avoided without compelling life-threatening bleeding.
level_2.C: Plasma can replace deficient ADAMTS13. Plasma infusion alone is not adequate definitive treatment for acute immune TTP when plasma exchange is available.
level_2.D: Rituximab can be an adjunct in immune TTP. It does not replace emergency plasma exchange and corticosteroids.

clinical_pearls: Draw ADAMTS13 before plasma exposure, then treat without waiting for the result.

content_sba.stem: A 40-year-old has a deep soil-contaminated puncture wound and no reliable history of receiving a tetanus-containing primary series. Wound cleaning and debridement have been performed.
content_sba.lead_in: Which prophylaxis is indicated?

choices.text: No tetanus-specific prophylaxis after wound cleaning
Give vaccine now; reserve immune globulin for wound infection
Give immune globulin now; start vaccine after wound healing
Give vaccine and immune globulin now at different sites

rationales.correct_answer: A dirty major wound with unknown vaccination history requires active vaccination plus passive protection with tetanus immune globulin.

A.why_tempting: Cleaning and debridement reduce contamination and are essential wound care.
A.why_wrong: They do not provide the active and passive tetanus protection indicated by this wound and history.

B.why_tempting: Vaccination is required for unknown or incomplete history.
B.why_wrong: Immune globulin is based on the dirty wound and vaccination history, not on later wound infection, and is also indicated now.

C.why_tempting: Immune globulin provides immediate antitoxin antibodies.
C.why_wrong: Active vaccination should begin now rather than wait for wound healing.

explanation.level_1: A dirty major wound with unknown vaccination history requires active vaccination plus passive protection with tetanus immune globulin.

level_2.A: Cleaning and debridement reduce contamination and are essential wound care. They do not provide the active and passive tetanus protection indicated by this wound and history.
level_2.B: Vaccination is required for unknown or incomplete history. Immune globulin is based on the dirty wound and vaccination history, not on later wound infection, and is also indicated now.
level_2.C: Immune globulin provides immediate antitoxin antibodies. Active vaccination should begin now rather than wait for wound healing.
level_2.D: A dirty major wound with unknown vaccination history requires active vaccination plus passive protection with tetanus immune globulin.

clinical_pearls: Vaccine and immune globulin serve different purposes and are administered at different sites.
Tetanus immune globulin is not indicated for a clean minor wound.

content_sba.stem: An adult with diabetic ketoacidosis has received initial fluid resuscitation. Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/L, urine output is present, and there is no advanced kidney failure.
content_sba.lead_in: Which action should occur next?

choices.text: Start intravenous insulin before replacing potassium
Replace potassium before starting intravenous insulin
Use subcutaneous insulin instead of potassium replacement

rationales.correct_answer: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia, so low potassium must be corrected before insulin is started.

A.why_tempting: Insulin is required to resolve ketoacidosis.
A.why_wrong: Starting it at this potassium level can provoke life-threatening hypokalemia.

C.why_wrong: Bicarbonate is not the priority and can aggravate the potassium decline.

D.why_tempting: Subcutaneous insulin is used in selected hyperglycemic management pathways.
D.why_wrong: Changing the insulin route does not remove the immediate danger of worsening this patient’s hypokalemia.

explanation.level_1: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia, so low potassium must be corrected before insulin is started.

level_2.A: Insulin is required to resolve ketoacidosis. Starting it at this potassium level can provoke life-threatening hypokalemia.
level_2.B: Insulin shifts potassium intracellularly and can precipitate dangerous hypokalemia, so low potassium must be corrected before insulin is started.
level_2.C: The patient is acidemic. Bicarbonate is not the priority and can aggravate the potassium decline.
level_2.D: Subcutaneous insulin is used in selected hyperglycemic management pathways. Changing the insulin route does not remove the immediate danger of worsening this patient’s hypokalemia.

clinical_pearls: Total-body potassium is depleted in DKA even when the initial serum concentration is normal or high.

level_2.D: Imaging the symptomatic region directly targets the apparent level. Whole-spine MRI is indicated because clinically important disease may be multifocal.

content_sba.stem: A patient with chronic kidney disease has a potassium concentration of 7.0 mmol/L, peaked T waves, and QRS widening.
content_sba.lead_in: Which medication should be given first to protect the myocardium?

rationales.correct_answer: Intravenous calcium rapidly antagonizes the cardiac electrophysiologic effects of hyperkalemia; urgent potassium-shifting and removal therapies must follow.

A.why_tempting: A potassium binder can remove potassium from the body.
A.why_wrong: It does not provide immediate cardiac membrane protection.

B.why_tempting: A loop diuretic may increase urinary potassium excretion.
B.why_wrong: Its effect is slower and depends on renal response.

D.why_tempting: Insulin with glucose rapidly shifts potassium intracellularly.
D.why_wrong: It lowers serum potassium but does not directly stabilize the myocardium.

explanation.level_1: Intravenous calcium rapidly antagonizes the cardiac electrophysiologic effects of hyperkalemia; urgent potassium-shifting and removal therapies must follow.

level_2.A: A potassium binder can remove potassium from the body. It does not provide immediate cardiac membrane protection.
level_2.B: A loop diuretic may increase urinary potassium excretion. Its effect is slower and depends on renal response.
level_2.C: Intravenous calcium rapidly antagonizes the cardiac electrophysiologic effects of hyperkalemia; urgent potassium-shifting and removal therapies must follow.
level_2.D: Insulin with glucose rapidly shifts potassium intracellularly. It lowers serum potassium but does not directly stabilize the myocardium.

clinical_pearls: Calcium improves electrical toxicity but does not lower the serum potassium concentration.
After protection, promptly shift potassium intracellularly and remove it from the body.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests the first physiologic goal when severe hyperkalemia causes ECG toxicity.

content_sba.stem: A 30-year-old at 30 weeks’ gestation had normal blood pressure before pregnancy and through 18 weeks. At today’s visit, blood pressure is 148/94 mm Hg and remains 150/96 mm Hg four hours later. A spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio is 0.35. She has no seizure and no severe headache, visual symptoms, dyspnea, or upper-abdominal pain.
content_sba.lead_in: Which diagnosis best fits this presentation?

rationales.correct_answer: New hypertension after 20 weeks together with proteinuria is the classic diagnostic pattern of preeclampsia; severe symptoms are not required for the diagnosis.

B.why_tempting: Gestational hypertension also begins after 20 weeks.
B.why_wrong: Gestational hypertension lacks proteinuria or another qualifying end-organ finding.

C.why_tempting: Chronic hypertension can be recognized during pregnancy.
C.why_wrong: It predates pregnancy or begins before 20 weeks rather than newly appearing at 30 weeks.

D.why_tempting: Eclampsia is the severe neurologic complication of preeclampsia.
D.why_wrong: Eclampsia requires a seizure, which is absent.

explanation.level_1: New hypertension after 20 weeks together with proteinuria is the classic diagnostic pattern of preeclampsia; severe symptoms are not required for the diagnosis.

level_2.A: New hypertension after 20 weeks together with proteinuria is the classic diagnostic pattern of preeclampsia; severe symptoms are not required for the diagnosis.
level_2.B: Gestational hypertension also begins after 20 weeks. Gestational hypertension lacks proteinuria or another qualifying end-organ finding.
level_2.C: Chronic hypertension can be recognized during pregnancy. It predates pregnancy or begins before 20 weeks rather than newly appearing at 30 weeks.
level_2.D: Eclampsia is the severe neurologic complication of preeclampsia. Eclampsia requires a seizure, which is absent.

clinical_pearls: Preeclampsia can first be detected on routine blood-pressure and urine assessment.
The absence of headache or visual symptoms does not exclude preeclampsia.

content_sba.stem: A 7-year-old develops high fever, cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis after a known exposure during a community outbreak. Small white lesions are seen on the buccal mucosa. Two days later, a maculopapular rash begins on the face and spreads toward the trunk and legs.
content_sba.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?

rationales.correct_answer: Fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash spreading from the face downward is the characteristic measles sequence.

A.why_tempting: Rubella is a vaccine-preventable febrile exanthem.
A.why_wrong: It is usually milder and does not produce the full three-C prodrome with Koplik spots.

B.why_tempting: Roseola also produces fever followed by rash.
B.why_wrong: Roseola usually affects younger children and the rash appears as the fever resolves.

D.why_tempting: Erythema infectiosum is another childhood viral exanthem.
D.why_wrong: It classically causes slapped cheeks and a lacy rash rather than Koplik spots.

explanation.level_1: Fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash spreading from the face downward is the characteristic measles sequence.

level_2.A: Rubella is a vaccine-preventable febrile exanthem. It is usually milder and does not produce the full three-C prodrome with Koplik spots.
level_2.B: Roseola also produces fever followed by rash. Roseola usually affects younger children and the rash appears as the fever resolves.
level_2.C: Fever with cough, coryza, conjunctivitis, Koplik spots, and a maculopapular rash spreading from the face downward is the characteristic measles sequence.
level_2.D: Erythema infectiosum is another childhood viral exanthem. It classically causes slapped cheeks and a lacy rash rather than Koplik spots.

content_sba.stem: A 27-year-old at approximately 7 weeks by last menstrual period has light vaginal bleeding and right-sided pelvic pain. A pregnancy test is positive. Transvaginal ultrasonography shows an empty uterus and a gestational sac containing a yolk sac in the right adnexa. She is hemodynamically stable.
content_sba.lead_in: Which diagnosis best explains these findings?

rationales.correct_answer: A gestational sac containing a yolk sac outside the uterus establishes an ectopic pregnancy.

A.why_tempting: Early pregnancy bleeding can occur with threatened loss.
A.why_wrong: The demonstrated adnexal pregnancy rules out a threatened intrauterine pregnancy.

C.why_tempting: Incomplete loss can produce bleeding and pain.
C.why_wrong: It involves passage and retention of intrauterine products, not an adnexal yolk sac.

D.why_tempting: Trophoblastic disease can present with abnormal early pregnancy findings.
D.why_wrong: It does not explain a discrete extrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac.

explanation.level_1: A gestational sac containing a yolk sac outside the uterus establishes an ectopic pregnancy.

level_2.A: Early pregnancy bleeding can occur with threatened loss. The demonstrated adnexal pregnancy rules out a threatened intrauterine pregnancy.
level_2.B: A gestational sac containing a yolk sac outside the uterus establishes an ectopic pregnancy.
level_2.C: Incomplete loss can produce bleeding and pain. It involves passage and retention of intrauterine products, not an adnexal yolk sac.
level_2.D: Trophoblastic disease can present with abnormal early pregnancy findings. It does not explain a discrete extrauterine gestational sac containing a yolk sac.

clinical_pearls: A positive pregnancy test does not establish pregnancy location.

content_sba.stem: An 11-year-old has two weeks of a progressively worsening cough. The cough now occurs in repeated rapid bursts, often at night, followed by a prolonged high-pitched inspiratory sound and occasional vomiting. Between episodes, the child is afebrile and the lung examination is unremarkable.
content_sba.lead_in: Which diagnosis is most likely?

rationales.correct_answer: Repeated paroxysms of rapid coughs followed by an inspiratory whoop and posttussive vomiting characterize the paroxysmal stage of pertussis.

A.why_wrong: It usually produces an abrupt systemic febrile illness rather than a staged prolonged paroxysmal cough.

B.why_tempting: Croup can produce a high-pitched inspiratory sound.
B.why_wrong: Croup produces a barking cough and stridor, chiefly in younger children, rather than posttussive emesis after cough bursts.

C.why_tempting: Mycoplasma can cause a persistent cough in school-aged children.
C.why_wrong: The whoop, paroxysms, and posttussive vomiting point more specifically to pertussis.

explanation.level_1: Repeated paroxysms of rapid coughs followed by an inspiratory whoop and posttussive vomiting characterize the paroxysmal stage of pertussis.

level_2.B: Croup can produce a high-pitched inspiratory sound. Croup produces a barking cough and stridor, chiefly in younger children, rather than posttussive emesis after cough bursts.
level_2.C: Mycoplasma can cause a persistent cough in school-aged children. The whoop, paroxysms, and posttussive vomiting point more specifically to pertussis.

content_sba.stem: A 68-year-old suddenly develops left lower facial droop, left arm drift, and slurred speech while eating breakfast 20 minutes ago. Bedside glucose is normal. Family members report that the deficits were maximal at onset.
content_sba.lead_in: Which acute diagnosis is most likely?

rationales.correct_answer: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with acute speech difficulty is a classic focal stroke presentation and requires emergency activation.

A.why_tempting: Bell palsy causes acute facial weakness.
A.why_wrong: It does not explain ipsilateral arm drift and dysarthria as a focal multidomain syndrome.

C.why_tempting: Migraine aura can mimic focal neurologic disease.
C.why_wrong: Aura more often evolves over minutes with spreading positive symptoms; these abrupt negative deficits favor stroke.

D.why_tempting: Postictal paresis can produce unilateral weakness.
D.why_wrong: The abrupt face-arm-speech syndrome without reported seizure activity is more consistent with acute stroke.

explanation.level_1: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with acute speech difficulty is a classic focal stroke presentation and requires emergency activation.

level_2.A: Bell palsy causes acute facial weakness. It does not explain ipsilateral arm drift and dysarthria as a focal multidomain syndrome.
level_2.B: Sudden unilateral face and arm weakness with acute speech difficulty is a classic focal stroke presentation and requires emergency activation.
level_2.C: Migraine aura can mimic focal neurologic disease. Aura more often evolves over minutes with spreading positive symptoms; these abrupt negative deficits favor stroke.
level_2.D: Postictal paresis can produce unilateral weakness. The abrupt face-arm-speech syndrome without reported seizure activity is more consistent with acute stroke.

clinical_pearls: Even resolving deficits can represent a transient ischemic attack and remain an emergency warning sign.
Most strokes are not preceded by headache.

content_sba.stem: A 24-year-old has eight days of persistently elevated and irritable mood, markedly increased activity, racing thoughts, pressured speech, and sleeping only two hours nightly without fatigue. Reckless spending has caused major financial and occupational consequences, and hospitalization is required for safety. No substance exposure or medical condition explains the change.
content_sba.lead_in: Which mood episode is represented?

rationales.correct_answer: The activated mood syndrome with decreased need for sleep and severe functional disruption requiring hospitalization represents a manic episode.

B.why_tempting: Hypomania shares elevated mood, energy, and reduced sleep need.
B.why_wrong: Marked impairment and hospitalization favor mania rather than hypomania.

C.why_tempting: Major depression can also produce serious functional consequences.
C.why_wrong: The stem shows activation rather than low mood or loss of interest.

D.why_tempting: Irritability and activation can occur with mixed features during a depressive episode.
D.why_wrong: No major depressive syndrome is described.

level_2.D: Irritability and activation can occur with mixed features during a depressive episode. No major depressive syndrome is described.

content_sba.stem: During a power outage, three family members who have been in a house with a fuel-burning generator operating in the attached garage develop headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion. None has fever. A conventional pulse oximeter shows a normal oxygen saturation.
content_sba.lead_in: Which poisoning best explains the cluster?

rationales.correct_answer: A shared enclosed-space combustion exposure with afebrile headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion in multiple people strongly suggests carbon monoxide poisoning; conventional pulse oximetry cannot exclude it.

A.why_tempting: Organophosphate exposure can make multiple people ill.
A.why_wrong: The expected cholinergic findings such as prominent secretions and bronchospasm are absent.

B.why_tempting: Methanol can cause neurologic and gastrointestinal symptoms.
B.why_wrong: It usually follows ingestion and often causes visual toxicity and metabolic acidosis rather than a generator-exhaust household cluster.

C.why_tempting: Cyanide can cause cellular hypoxia after smoke exposure.
C.why_wrong: The generator setting and shared household symptom pattern point more specifically to carbon monoxide.

explanation.level_1: A shared enclosed-space combustion exposure with afebrile headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion in multiple people strongly suggests carbon monoxide poisoning; conventional pulse oximetry cannot exclude it.

level_2.A: Organophosphate exposure can make multiple people ill. The expected cholinergic findings such as prominent secretions and bronchospasm are absent.
level_2.B: Methanol can cause neurologic and gastrointestinal symptoms. It usually follows ingestion and often causes visual toxicity and metabolic acidosis rather than a generator-exhaust household cluster.
level_2.C: Cyanide can cause cellular hypoxia after smoke exposure. The generator setting and shared household symptom pattern point more specifically to carbon monoxide.
level_2.D: A shared enclosed-space combustion exposure with afebrile headache, dizziness, nausea, and confusion in multiple people strongly suggests carbon monoxide poisoning; conventional pulse oximetry cannot exclude it.

content_sba.stem: A 58-year-old reports that an 8-mm pigmented lesion has enlarged and changed color over three months. Examination shows asymmetry, an irregular border, and brown, black, and red areas within the lesion.

B.why_tempting: Dermatofibroma is a common skin lesion.

level_2.D: Basal cell carcinoma is common and can ulcerate. It more often appears pearly or translucent; this changing multicolored pattern makes melanoma the priority to exclude.

content_sba.stem: A 48-year-old adult with no known hypertension is asymptomatic during routine U.S. primary-care screening. Properly performed office measurements are 150/94 and 148/92 mm Hg, with no findings suggesting hypertensive emergency or acute target-organ injury.

content_sba.stem: A 72-year-old develops a new unilateral temporal headache with scalp tenderness and jaw pain while chewing. Yesterday, vision in one eye dimmed for several minutes.

C.why_tempting: Cluster headache causes severe unilateral pain.
C.why_wrong: It produces short attacks with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms, not jaw claudication.

D.why_tempting: Tension headache is common in adults.
D.why_wrong: It does not account for jaw claudication or transient monocular visual loss.

explanation.level_1: In an adult older than 50, a new temporal headache with jaw claudication and transient monocular visual symptoms is the characteristic high-risk giant cell arteritis pattern.

level_2.A: Migraine aura can cause transient visual symptoms and headache. New onset at this age with scalp tenderness and jaw claudication strongly favors giant cell arteritis.
level_2.B: In an adult older than 50, a new temporal headache with jaw claudication and transient monocular visual symptoms is the characteristic high-risk giant cell arteritis pattern.
level_2.C: Cluster headache causes severe unilateral pain. It produces short attacks with ipsilateral autonomic symptoms, not jaw claudication.
level_2.D: Tension headache is common in adults. It does not account for jaw claudication or transient monocular visual loss.

clinical_pearls: Visual symptoms signal threatened permanent vision loss and require urgent action.
Inflammatory markers support but do not alone establish the diagnosis.
level_3.board_relevance: Tests a high-risk headache diagnosis from age and ischemic features.
level_3.interview_relevance: Educational oral-reasoning relevance only; not validated for residency selection: Assesses whether the candidate recognizes time-sensitive vision risk.
common_traps: Calling a new older-adult headache migraine
Treating inflammatory markers as a standalone diagnosis
level_3.memory_aid: Over 50, chewing ache, eye at risk.
